title: Animals around us: coverings, legs, wings and fins

summary.text: A crow stands on two legs, a cat on four and an ant on six. Animals are covered in hair or fur, feathers, scales, a shell or bare skin. They move with legs, wings, fins, or their whole body. You count an ant's legs, look closely at your own hair and nails, and build a dough animal to test how many legs a body needs to stand without help. You also sort the animals you see into pets, farm animals and wild animals, and find that many wild animals live right next to us.
summary.art: A city balcony with a crow on the railing, a cat on the step below and a line of ants on the floor, and a girl kneeling to count the ants' legs.

intro.hook: A crow on the window ledge has two legs. The cat downstairs has four. The ant on the kitchen floor has six. Why do animals come with so many different numbers of legs?
intro.text: Animals around us look very different. A crow is covered in feathers, a cat in fur, a gecko in tiny scales and you in skin and hair. A fish swims with fins, a crow flies with wings, and a snake slides along with no legs at all. Scientists compare animals by looking at their bodies, part by part. In this unit you count legs, compare coverings and test how many legs a body needs to stand without help.
intro.art: Three animals in a row, drawn simply: a crow on two legs, a cat on four legs and an ant on six legs, with a number under each.

outcomes: By the end I can sort animals by their body covering: hair or fur, feathers, scales, a shell, or bare skin.
By the end I can count and compare legs, and name an animal with no legs, two, four, six and eight legs.
By the end I can say which animals move with legs, wings, fins or their whole body, and that some use more than one.
By the end I can explain why a body with three or four legs stands still easily, and how two-legged animals keep their balance.
By the end I can tell a pet, a farm animal and a wild animal apart, and say that wild animals live near us too.
By the end I can say that humans are animals too: mammals with hair, two legs and no wings.

terms.meaning: A body covering is what covers the outside of an animal's body.
terms.example: A crow's covering is feathers. A cat's covering is fur. Your covering is skin and hair.
terms.art: Four close-up circles: a black crow feather, ginger cat fur, a gecko's bumpy scales and a child's arm with tiny hairs.

terms.meaning: Fur is thick, soft hair that covers an animal's body. Hair grows out of the skin.
terms.example: A dog, a goat and a squirrel have fur. You have hair on your head and tiny hairs on your arms.
terms.art: A striped palm squirrel with fluffy fur sitting on a wall.

terms.meaning: Feathers are the light covering of a bird. Every bird has feathers, and no other animal alive today has them.
terms.example: A pigeon, a peacock and a hen all have feathers.
terms.art: A grey pigeon feather lying on a balcony floor.

terms.meaning: Scales are small, hard, flat plates that cover the skin of some animals.
terms.example: A fish, a snake and a gecko have scales.
terms.art: A silver fish and a green snake side by side, with their scales drawn clearly.

terms.meaning: A shell is a hard case that covers and protects a soft body.
terms.example: A snail and a tortoise each carry a shell.
terms.art: A garden snail and a small tortoise, each with their shell.

terms.meaning: Wings are the body parts an animal flaps to fly.
terms.example: A crow, a bat and a butterfly have wings.
terms.art: A crow, a fruit bat and a butterfly in the sky, wings spread.

terms.meaning: Fins are flat body parts that a fish uses to swim, steer and stay upright in water.
terms.example: A fish has a tail fin, a fin on the back and fins on the sides.
terms.art: A goldfish from the side, with each fin coloured a little darker.

terms.meaning: A mammal is an animal with hair or fur, whose mother feeds her babies on milk.
terms.example: A cow, a dog, a bat, an elephant and you are all mammals.
terms.art: A mother goat feeding her kid, and a mother holding her baby, side by side.

terms.meaning: Balance means keeping your body steady so that you do not fall over.
terms.example: When you stand on one foot, your foot and ankle keep moving a little to keep your balance.
terms.art: A girl standing on one foot with her arms out, and small curved lines around her ankle.

terms.meaning: A pet is an animal that a family keeps at home and looks after.
terms.example: A cat that sleeps at home and is fed every day is a pet.
terms.art: A girl filling a water bowl for a black-and-white cat in a flat.

terms.meaning: A farm animal is an animal that people keep for milk, eggs, wool or work.
terms.example: A cow, a goat, a hen and a buffalo are farm animals.
terms.art: A woman milking a cow in a village shed, with hens pecking near her feet.

terms.meaning: A wild animal lives on their own, and finds their own food and home.
terms.example: A crow, a gecko on the wall and a tiger in the forest are wild animals.
terms.art: A gecko on a wall beside a tube light, catching a moth.

explanations.context: This card is about what covers an animal's body, and what the covering is made of.
explanations.definition: A body covering is the outside layer of an animal's body: hair or fur, feathers, scales, a shell, or bare skin.
explanations.description: Most mammals are covered in hair or fur. Birds are covered in feathers. Fish, snakes and lizards have scales. Snails and tortoises carry a shell. Frogs and earthworms have bare, damp skin. Your hair and nails, a crow's feathers, a cow's horns and a gecko's scales are all made of the same tough material. It is called keratin. Fish scales are different: they are made of a bony material.
examples: A goat is covered in fur.
A peacock is covered in feathers.
A gecko is covered in tiny bumpy scales.
A frog has bare, damp skin.
explanations.art: Five boxes in a row: fur, a feather, scales, a snail shell and smooth frog skin, each with a small drawing of an animal next to the box.

explanations.context: This card is about how many legs different animals have.
explanations.definition: Animals can have no legs, two, four, six, eight or many legs.
explanations.description: Snakes, fish and earthworms have no legs. Birds and humans walk on two legs. Dogs, cows, frogs and geckos have four. Every adult insect, such as an ant, a fly or a butterfly, has six legs. Spiders have eight legs, so a spider is not an insect. Centipedes and millipedes have many legs. One millipede in Western Australia has 1,306 legs!
examples: A sparrow has 2 legs.
A buffalo has 4 legs.
A mosquito has 6 legs.
A spider has 8 legs.
explanations.art: A row of animals from fewest to most legs: an earthworm, a sparrow, a cow, an ant, a spider and a millipede.

explanations.context: This card is about the body parts animals use to fly and to swim.
explanations.definition: Wings are body parts that an animal flaps to fly. Fins are flat body parts that a fish uses to swim and steer.
explanations.description: Birds, bats and most insects have wings. A bat is not a bird: bats have fur and feed their babies milk, so bats are mammals. Some birds have wings but do not fly, such as the penguin and the ostrich. A fish has a tail fin that pushes them forward. Fins on the back and belly stop the fish from rolling over. Fins on the sides help them steer and stop. Dolphins and whales have fins too, but they breathe air and feed their babies milk. They are mammals, not fish.
examples: A crow has wings and two legs.
A butterfly has wings and six legs.
A fish has fins and no legs.
A dolphin has fins and is a mammal.
explanations.art: A fish with arrows: the tail fin pushing, the fin on the back keeping the fish upright, and a side fin steering.

explanations.context: This card explains the Dough Legs test, where a dough animal stood on three or four legs but fell over on two.
explanations.definition: A body stands still by itself when its weight is above the space between its feet. Three feet, spread out, make that space a triangle.
explanations.description: One leg or two legs give a body only a small place to stand, so the body tips over. Three legs, spread out, make a triangle, so a stool with three legs stands. Four or six legs stand easily too. Humans and birds stand on two legs, and keep their balance by moving all the time. Your feet feel the floor, your ears feel you tilt and your eyes see you lean. Your muscles then tighten and loosen to catch you. With your eyes shut, you sway more, so you feel this more.
examples: A camera stand has three legs.
A cow standing in the road has four legs on the ground.
A crow standing on one leg keeps adjusting their foot on the wire.
explanations.art: Three dough animals on a board: one on two legs falling over, one on three legs standing, one on four legs standing, with a triangle drawn between the three feet.

explanations.concept: Pets, farm animals and wild animals
explanations.context: This card is about the different ways animals live with people, or without them.
explanations.definition: A pet lives with a family who look after them. A farm animal is kept for milk, eggs, wool or work. A wild animal lives on their own and finds their own food.
explanations.description: Wild animals do not only live in forests. Crows, pigeons, squirrels, geckos and ants are wild animals that live in cities. In Mumbai, leopards live in a forest park inside the city. Being a pet depends on how an animal lives, not on what kind of animal they are. A parrot in the forest is wild. In India, the Wildlife Protection Act of 1972 makes it against the law to catch or keep wild Indian birds, such as parakeets and munias. Some animals, like street dogs and temple cows, are fed by many people but belong to no one family. People argue about what to call them.
examples: A cat at home is a pet.
A buffalo kept for milk is a farm animal.
A crow on the water tank is a wild animal.
A street dog fed by the whole lane is a community dog.
explanations.art: Three circles: a girl with her pet cat, a woman with a goat, and a crow on a water tank on a building.

explanations.concept: Sorting by more than one part
explanations.context: This card is about tricky animals that do not fit one simple rule.
explanations.definition: Scientists sort animals by looking at many body parts together, not just one.
explanations.description: Wings alone do not make a bird: butterflies and bats have wings too. Fins alone do not make a fish: dolphins have fins. Scales alone do not make a reptile: the Indian pangolin is a mammal covered in scales, and the mother feeds her baby on milk. So scientists look at the covering, the legs, how the animal breathes and how the babies are fed, all together. Humans are mammals: you have hair, you breathed air from your first minute, and babies drink milk.
examples: A bat has wings and fur, so a bat is a mammal.
A pangolin has scales and drinks milk as a baby, so a pangolin is a mammal.
A penguin has wings and feathers but cannot fly, and a penguin is a bird.
explanations.art: An Indian pangolin curled half into a ball, with her baby holding on to her tail.

explanations.context: This card is about something scientists still argue about.
explanations.description: Fossils show that some dinosaurs had feathers, millions of years before birds flew. So feathers did not first grow for flying. Scientists have different ideas about what the first feathers did.
examples: Fossils of small feathered dinosaurs have been found in China since 1996.
Baby chicks have soft fluffy feathers that keep them warm.

perspectives.explanation: The first feathers kept small dinosaurs warm, like the fluff on a chick.
The first feathers were for showing off, to attract a mate or warn a rival, like a peacock's tail.
Both were true, and feathers were used for flying only much later.

explanations.art: A small dinosaur covered in fluffy feathers, standing beside a hen.

agreed.text: Every bird has feathers, and no other animal alive today has feathers.
agreed.evidence: Scientists have studied about 11,000 kinds of birds. Every one has feathers. No mammal, fish, reptile or insect alive today has them.

agreed.text: Every adult insect has six legs.
agreed.evidence: Ants, flies, bees, beetles and butterflies all have six legs as adults. Spiders have eight legs, which is one reason spiders are not insects.
Humans have hair, breathe air with lungs and feed babies on milk, like cows, dogs and bats.

challenging.claim: Anything with fins that lives in water is a fish.
challenging.who: A very common idea, held for hundreds of years
challenging.for: Most animals with fins that live in water are fish, like rohu, sardines and goldfish.
challenging.against: Dolphins and whales have fins, but they breathe air and feed their babies milk. The river dolphin of the Ganga and the Brahmaputra is a mammal.
challenging.context: This card is about a mistake people made for a long time.

challenging.claim: Wild animals live only in forests.
challenging.who: A common idea among children and grown-ups
challenging.for: Tigers, elephants and many other wild animals do live in forests.
challenging.against: Crows, pigeons, squirrels, geckos and ants are wild, and live in cities. In Mumbai, leopards live in Sanjay Gandhi National Park, inside the city.
challenging.context: This card is about where wild animals live.

challenging.claim: Bats are a kind of bird, because bats have wings.
challenging.who: An old idea, found in many old books
challenging.for: Bats have wings and fly, like birds.
challenging.against: Bats have fur, not feathers. Bat babies drink their mother's milk. So bats are mammals.
challenging.context: This card is about a tricky animal.

challenging.claim: Dogs became pets because people caught wolf pups and tamed them.
challenging.for: Wolf pups raised by people can become friendly with people.
challenging.against: Other scientists think the friendliest wolves came close to people's camps by themselves, to eat scraps. Over many generations, these wolves became dogs. Nobody knows for sure which story is right.
challenging.context: This card is about how dogs and people came to live together.

big_questions.q: When you stand still, which parts of you are working? Who decides each tiny shift?
big_questions.hint: Remember standing with your eyes shut. Did you decide to move your ankle, or did your ankle move by itself?

big_questions.q: Is a pet a kind of animal, or a kind of friendship between an animal and a family?
big_questions.hint: A parrot can be wild in the forest. A street dog can be fed by a whole lane. What makes an animal a pet?

big_questions.q: We sort animals by their bodies. How might a crow sort the animals they see?
big_questions.hint: A crow might sort animals into ones that are dangerous and ones that are not, or ones that share food and ones that do not.

big_questions.q: If you met an animal with feathers and four legs, what group would you put them in?
big_questions.hint: No animal like this is alive today. Would you make a new group, or change the rules of the old groups?

big_questions.q: Does the gecko on your wall think of your home as their home too?
big_questions.hint: The gecko was there before you noticed. The gecko finds food, hides and sleeps there.

story.title: The Clicking in the Hall
story.note: A made-up story. House geckos really do make clicking calls, eat moths near lights, grip with tiny hairs on their toes and can drop their tails.
text: Every night that week, something in Nila's flat went tchk, tchk, tchk.
Nila was seven. She lived on the fourth floor of a building in Bengaluru, with Amma, her grandmother Ajji and her little brother Kabir, who was five.
'There is a mouse in the shoe rack,' said Kabir. 'A big one.'
'Maybe,' said Amma, tying her bank badge on. 'Or maybe not. You two can find out.'
Nila decided to find out the way a scientist would. She took a notebook and wrote CLUES at the top.
Clue one: the sound came at night, from near the tube light in the hall. Clue two: on the window ledge, Nila found three tiny droppings. Each one was dark, with a little white tip at one end.
That evening Hema aunty came over from the flat opposite. Hema aunty helped at an animal rescue centre on weekends, and she knew a lot about animals.
Nila showed her the notebook. Hema aunty read it carefully.
'Before you guess,' said Hema aunty, 'think about the bodies of the animals that might live here. What covers them? How many legs do they have? What do they leave behind?'
Nila drew three boxes. In the first she drew a mouse. 'A mouse has fur and four legs,' she said. 'A mouse squeaks.'
In the second she drew a cockroach. 'A cockroach has six legs and a hard, shiny case, and wings,' said Nila. 'I have never heard a cockroach go tchk.'

'Now look at the droppings,' said Hema aunty. 'Mouse droppings are dark all over. Birds and lizards are different. They do not pass wee as water. Their wee comes out as a white paste, with the dropping. That is the white tip.'
'A bird can't get into the shoe rack,' said Kabir. 'The door is shut.'
'So,' said Nila slowly, 'our visitor is a lizard.'
That night, all four of them sat in the dark hall. Ajji held the torch. They waited and waited. Kabir nearly fell asleep.
Then Ajji switched the tube light on.
On the wall beside the light was a small, pale animal with four legs and a long tail. A moth fluttered near the light. The animal ran up the wall in a flash, and the moth was gone.
'Halli!' whispered Kabir. That is the Kannada word for a house gecko.
The gecko ran across the ceiling, upside down, and stopped. The gecko did not fall.
'How do her feet stick?' asked Kabir.
'Under her toes are millions of tiny hairs,' said Hema aunty. 'They are so small and so many that they hold on to the ceiling.'
Nila looked through Ajji's reading glasses. The gecko's skin was covered in tiny bumps. 'Scales,' said Nila. 'Like a snake. But with four legs.'
Just then the gecko went tchk, tchk, tchk.
Everyone laughed. The mystery was solved.
'Can she be our pet?' asked Kabir. 'We can call her Chikki.'

Hema aunty smiled. 'Chikki lives in your home, but she is a wild animal. Nobody feeds her. She catches her own moths and mosquitoes. She comes and goes as she likes. My cat Pepper is a pet. I give Pepper food and water every day, and take her to the vet.'
'So Chikki is our wild neighbour,' said Nila.
'Will she bite me?' asked Kabir.

'House geckos are harmless,' said Hema aunty. 'But do not try to catch her. If a gecko is grabbed, her tail can come off, so that she can run away. A new tail grows back, but it is never quite the same.'

The next morning, Nila made a new page in her notebook. She drew the mouse, the cockroach and the gecko. She drew the crow on the window ledge, with feathers, two legs and wings. Then she drew herself, with hair, skin, two legs and no wings.
'Why are you on the page?' asked Kabir.
'Because I am an animal too,' said Nila. 'A mammal, like the mouse. Hema aunty said so.'
That night the tube light went on, and the moths came, and so did Chikki.
'Good night, wild neighbour,' whispered Nila.
story.epiphany: For the parent: Nila tells animals apart by their bodies: what covers them, how many legs they have and what they leave behind. She also learns that an animal can live in your home and still be wild.
ask: Which clues helped Nila find out that the animal was a gecko and not a mouse?
Why is Chikki a wild animal, even though she lives in Nila's home?
Why did Nila draw herself on the same page as the animals?

printables.title: 5 covering mats to lay on the floor

rules: Before you play, share the cards and draw a quick animal under each name, so that a child who cannot read yet can play. A simple shape is enough.
Lay the five covering mats in a circle on the floor.
Mix the cards and put them face down in a pile.
One player turns over the top card and reads the name aloud.
Everyone races to put a hand on the right mat. A hand on a wrong mat means you sit out that card.
Turn the card over to check. The first hand on the right mat wins the card.
When the pile is finished, the player with the most cards wins. If two players have the same number, they both win.

flow.do: 1. Share the 24 cards between you and draw a quick animal on each. 2. Lay the five mats in a circle.
flow.say: Let's draw the animals first. I will draw some and you draw some.
flow.kid: Draw an animal on your cards. Then lay out the five mats.

flow.do: 1. Take turns turning over a card. 2. Race to the right mat. 3. Turn the card over to check.
flow.say: Crow! Which mat? Quick!
flow.kid: Turn over a card. Slap the right mat. Check the back.

ask.q: The bat has wings. Why does the bat go on the hair or fur mat?
good: Because a bat has fur.
Because a bat is a mammal, not a bird.

flow.parent: The tricky cards are the bat, the pangolin, the butterfly, the ant and the dolphin. Let the race stop for these, and talk about them.

flow.do: Count the cards. Then pick up the pangolin card and ask the check question.
flow.say: Who has the most cards? Now, a tricky one.
flow.kid: Count your cards. Who has the most?

check.q: A pangolin is covered in scales, and the mother feeds her baby milk. What is a pangolin?
check.why: Animals whose mothers feed them milk are mammals. A pangolin is a mammal with scales instead of fur. One body part alone does not tell you the group.

games.title: Build-a-Beast
games.context: This is a drawing game about how animal bodies go together. Players pick a covering, a number of legs and an extra part, draw the beast, and then try to name a real animal with that body.

printables.title: Beast sheet: a box to draw in, and a line for the real animal
items: A real animal with this body:

rules: Put the covering cards, leg cards and extra cards in three face-down piles.
On your turn, take one card from each pile. Put the cards back and mix the piles after each turn.
Everyone draws a beast with that body in two minutes, and gives the beast a name.
Then everyone tries to name a real animal with that body. Each player who names a real animal earns one point.
If nobody can name one, talk about why. Is there really no animal like this? That earns everyone one point.
After three turns each, the player with the most points wins. If you are tied, you all win.

flow.do: Lay out the three piles. Give everyone a pencil and a beast sheet.
flow.say: We will make beasts. Take one card from each pile.
flow.kid: Take one card from each pile.

flow.do: 1. Read the three cards aloud. 2. Draw for two minutes. 3. Then name real animals. 4. Play three turns each, taking turns to pick the cards.
flow.say: Feathers, two legs and wings. Draw your beast. Now, is there a real animal like this?
flow.kid: Draw your beast. Can you name a real animal like this?

ask.q: Feathers and four legs. Is there a real animal like this?
good: No. Every animal with feathers is a bird, and birds have two legs.
Not today. Birds have two legs and two wings.

flow.parent: Some mixes have many answers (feathers, 2 legs, wings: any bird). Some have none (feathers and 4 legs, fur and 6 legs). Others surprise: scales and no legs is a snake or a fish, and scales with 4 legs is a gecko or a crocodile.

flow.do: Look at all the beasts together. Ask the check question.
flow.say: Which beast was the strangest? Could any of them really live?
flow.kid: Show your beasts. Which one could really live?

check.q: Which mix belongs to a real animal?
options: Hair, two legs and no wings
check.why: Hair, two legs and no wings is a human. No animal alive today has feathers and four legs, and no animal with fur has six legs.

experiments.title: Dough Legs: how many legs does a body need to stand?
experiments.context: In this experiment you make an animal body from atta dough, and give the body 1, 2, 3, 4 and then 6 legs. You test which ones stand by themselves. Then you stand on two legs with your eyes shut, and feel what your own feet do.
experiments.question: How many legs does a body need to stand still without help? And how do we stand on only two?
experiments.predict: Guess first. How many legs will the dough animal need to stand without help without falling over? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: We use the same dough body and legs of the same length every time. Only the number of legs changes. We let go and count to five each time, and try each number twice, because one try can be luck.

materials.item: atta dough, made from about 3 tablespoons of atta and a little water, or play clay
materials.qty: a ball the size of a lime

materials.item: toothpicks, ear buds, or broom sticks cut to the same length, about 6 cm
a wooden board, a thick book or a table top
a pencil and paper for the results

experiments.safety: Toothpicks have sharp points. A grown-up cuts any sticks, and nobody waves the legs near eyes. Stand near a wall or a grown-up when you shut your eyes.

schedule.what: Make a dough body. Test it on 1, 2, 3, 4 and 6 legs. Then stand with your eyes shut and feel your feet.

experiments.record: Fill in the results table. Draw the dough animals that stood and the ones that fell.

flow.do: 1. Roll the dough into a ball, then press it into a short, fat egg shape. 2. Push one leg into the middle of the bottom.
flow.say: This is our dough animal's body. Now the body has one leg.
flow.kid: Roll the dough into a fat egg. Push in one leg.

flow.do: Ask your child to guess and to say why. Write the guess on the paper.
flow.say: How many legs will our animal need to stand without help? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess. How many legs does it need to stand? Why?

good: Two, because I stand on two legs.
Four, because a cow and a dog stand on four.

flow.parent: Many children guess two, because they stand on two legs themselves. Do not correct the guess. The test will answer it.

flow.do: 1. Stand the body on the board on one leg and let go. 2. Count to five. 3. Write down what happened. 4. Add a second leg and test again. 5. Then test three legs, four legs and six legs. 6. Try each number twice.
flow.say: Let go gently and count to five. Did the animal stand, wobble or fall?
flow.kid: Let go. Count to five. Did it stand or fall?

good: The dough animal fell over, forward or backward.
It fell every time unless I held it.

flow.parent: Push the legs in so they spread out a little, like the legs of a stool. With one or two legs, the body tips over every time. With three legs spread out, it stands. Four and six stand easily. If three legs fall, spread them wider and keep the body in the middle.

flow.do: 1. Take out all but two legs. 2. Press a flat dough foot, about as wide as a coin, onto the end of each leg. 3. Test again.
flow.say: Birds stand on two legs with wide, spread toes. Will big feet help our animal stand on two legs?
flow.kid: Give the two legs big flat feet. Does it stand now?
flow.parent: With big flat feet, the two-legged animal often stands, but wobbles. Wide feet give the body more floor to stand on.

flow.do: 1. Your child stands on both feet, near a wall, and shuts their eyes for 20 seconds. 2. Ask what the feet and ankles feel. 3. Then try one foot, eyes open, for 10 seconds.
flow.say: Stand still and shut your eyes. Don't move on purpose. What do your feet and ankles feel?
flow.kid: Stand near a wall. Shut your eyes. What do your feet do?

ask.q: What did you feel in your feet?
good: My toes pressed down and let go.
My ankles kept moving a tiny bit.
I kept swaying and stopping.

flow.parent: Your child will feel the toes press, the ankles tighten and loosen, and the body sway a little. Shutting the eyes makes the sway bigger, so the corrections are easier to feel. Standing on one foot makes them bigger still.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what they think, what they saw, and why.
flow.say: So, how many legs did the dough animal need? And how do you stand on two?
flow.kid: How many legs did it need? How do you stand on two?

ask.q: Why can you stand on two legs, when the dough animal could not?
good: Because my feet and ankles keep moving to catch me.
Because my body keeps balancing, and the dough does not.

flow.parent: A strong answer uses the test: the dough fell on two legs but stood on three, and their own feet kept making tiny moves. Now read the card on standing and balance together.

check.q: The dough animal fell over on two legs, but stood on three. Why can you stand on two legs?
options: Because your feet and ankles keep making tiny moves to keep you up
check.why: Your body keeps catching itself before you tip, many times while you stand. The dough cannot do that, so it needs three legs in a triangle.

setup.caption: 1. Make a dough body.

setup.caption: 2. Test 1, 2, 3, 4 and 6 legs. Let go and count to five.

setup.caption: 3. Stand with your eyes shut. Feel your feet and ankles.

experiments.title: Roll Stopper: what does a fin do?
experiments.context: In this experiment you float a plastic bottle in a bucket and make it roll. Then you tape a fin to the bottle and test again. This shows what the fins on a fish's back and belly do.
experiments.question: Does a fin stop a floating bottle from rolling over?
experiments.predict: Guess first. When we add a fin, will the bottle roll more, less or the same? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: We use the same bottle, the same water and the same flick each time. The only change is the fin. We try three flicks each way, because one flick can be harder than another.

materials.item: a small empty plastic bottle with a cap, 500 ml or smaller, with the label taken off
a bucket, a big vessel or a sink, filled with water
a stiff piece of plastic about 12 cm long and 4 cm wide, cut from an old food box lid
sticky tape
a bindi or a sticker, to mark one side of the bottle

experiments.safety: A grown-up cuts the plastic. Wipe up spilled water so nobody slips.

schedule.what: Float the bottle. Flick it and count the turns. Tape on a fin. Flick and count again.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw the bottle with and without the fin.

flow.do: 1. Pour water into the bottle until it is about a quarter full. 2. Close the cap tight. 3. Stick a bindi on the side. 4. Lay the bottle on its side in the bucket.
flow.say: This bottle is our fish body. The bindi helps us count each time it turns over.
flow.kid: Put a little water in the bottle. Stick on a bindi. Float it.

flow.do: Brush a finger quickly across the top of the bottle, from one side to the other. Count how many times the bindi goes round. Do it three times.
flow.say: Flick the top of the bottle. Count how many times the bindi comes round.
flow.kid: Flick the bottle. Count the turns.
flow.parent: Without a fin, the bottle usually rolls round one to three times with each flick.

flow.do: Ask your child to guess and to say why.
flow.say: Now we will tape a fin along the bottom. Will the bottle roll more, less or the same? Why?
flow.kid: We will add a fin. Will it roll more or less? Why?

flow.do: 1. Dry the bottle. 2. Tape the plastic strip along the length of the bottle, standing out like a fin. 3. Float the bottle with the fin pointing down into the water.
flow.say: A fish has a fin on the back and one underneath. Our fin goes underneath, in the water.
flow.kid: Tape the fin on. Float it with the fin down.

flow.do: Flick the bottle the same way, three times. Count the turns.
flow.say: Flick it just like before. What happens now?
flow.kid: Flick it the same way. Count the turns.

good: The bottle rocked and stopped.
It did not roll over at all.

flow.parent: With the fin, the bottle rocks a little and stops. The fin has to push a lot of water out of the way to turn, so it hardly turns.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what they think, what they saw, and why.
flow.say: So what does a fin on a fish's back or belly do?
flow.kid: What does a fin do for a fish?

ask.q: Why did the fin stop the rolling?
good: Because the fin pushes against the water.
Because the water holds the fin back.

flow.parent: A strong answer uses the counts: no fin, the bottle rolled. With a fin, it stopped. Fins on a fish's back and belly do the same job. They push against the water and keep the fish upright.

check.q: With a fin, the bottle stopped rolling. What does the fin on a fish's back do?
options: Keeps the fish from rolling over
check.why: A fin pushes against the water when the fish starts to roll, so the fish stays upright. The tail fin is the one that pushes a fish forward.

setup.art: A small plastic bottle with a red bindi, floating on its side in a bucket of water, and a child's finger flicking the top.
setup.caption: 1. Float the bottle and flick it. Count the turns.

setup.art: The same bottle with a flat plastic strip taped along the bottom, pointing down into the water.
setup.caption: 2. Tape on a fin and flick again.

activities.title: Count an Ant's Legs
activities.context: In this activity you put out a few grains of sugar for ants. Then you look closely and count an ant's legs, using a phone camera to zoom in.

materials.item: a few grains of sugar
a small white plate or a sheet of white paper
a phone with a camera, or a magnifying glass

schedule.what: An hour before, put sugar out for ants. Then zoom in and count an ant's legs and feelers.

activities.record: Draw the ant with every leg. Write the number of legs.

flow.do: 1. About an hour before, put a pinch of sugar on a white plate. 2. Put the plate on the floor where you have seen ants.
flow.say: Ants find sugar fast. Let's give them some and see who comes.
flow.kid: Put sugar on a plate where the ants walk.

flow.do: Ask your child to guess before looking.
flow.say: How many legs do you think an ant has? Why?
flow.kid: How many legs does an ant have? Guess!

flow.do: 1. Hold the phone close and zoom in on one ant at the sugar. 2. Take a photo. 3. Zoom in on the photo and count the legs together.
flow.say: Let's count every leg. Point to each one as you count.
flow.kid: Zoom in. Point to each leg. Count!

ask.q: How many legs did you count?
good: Six legs.
Three on each side.

flow.parent: An ant has six legs, three on each side, and two feelers called antennae on the head. Children sometimes count the feelers as legs. If no ants come, try again later, or look at an ant on the kitchen counter or the balcony.

flow.do: Compare the ant's legs with your child's legs and a crow's legs.
flow.say: You have two legs. A crow has two. The ant has six. Why might an ant need more legs?
flow.kid: You have 2 legs. The ant has 6. Why so many?

ask.q: Why might six legs help an ant?
good: To walk fast and not fall over.
To carry food and hold on to walls.

check.q: How many legs does an ant have?
check.why: An ant has six legs, three on each side. Every adult insect has six legs. The two feelers on the head are not legs.

setup.caption: 1. Put out sugar for the ants.

setup.art: A phone screen showing a zoomed-in ant with six legs and two feelers, and a child's finger pointing at one leg.
setup.caption: 2. Zoom in and count the legs.

activities.title: Up Close: my hair, skin and nails
activities.context: In this activity you look closely at your own body covering: the hair on your arm, your skin and your nails. You find out what they are made of.

materials.item: a phone with a camera, or a magnifying glass
a feather, if you have found one on the balcony or a walk

activities.safety: If you use a feather you found outside, hold it by the end and wash your hands after.

schedule.what: Zoom in on your arm hair, skin and nails. Compare them with a feather, if you have one.

activities.record: Draw your arm hair and a nail, as big as you saw them.

flow.do: 1. Zoom in on the inside of your child's arm with the phone camera. 2. Then zoom in on a fingernail.
flow.say: Look closely at your arm. Can you see tiny hairs? Where do they come out of?
flow.kid: Zoom in on your arm. Find the tiny hairs.

ask.q: Where does each hair come out of?
good: Out of a tiny hole in my skin.
Out of my skin.

flow.do: If you have a feather, zoom in on it and compare with the hair.
flow.say: A feather grows out of a bird's skin, as your hair grows out of yours. How are they the same? How are they different?
flow.kid: Look at the feather. How is it like your hair?
flow.parent: Your hair, your nails, a bird's feathers, a cow's horns and a gecko's scales are all made of the same tough material, called keratin. Fish scales are made of a bony material instead.

flow.do: Talk about coverings.
flow.say: Your covering is skin and hair. Which animals have a covering made of the same material as your nails?
flow.kid: Which animals are covered in the same material as your nails?

check.q: Your nails and a crow's feathers are made of the same material. What is it called?
check.why: Hair, nails, feathers, horns and the scales of snakes and lizards are all made of keratin, shaped in different ways.

setup.art: A phone camera zoomed in on a child's forearm, showing tiny hairs coming out of the skin.
setup.caption: 1. Zoom in on your arm hair.

setup.art: A grey pigeon feather beside a child's hand, both seen up close.
setup.caption: 2. Compare with a feather, if you have one.

activities.title: Move Like Them
activities.context: In this activity you move the way different animals move: on two legs, on four, with wings, with fins, and with no legs at all.

materials.item: a clear space on the floor

schedule.what: Act out how six animals move. Guess which animal each person is.

activities.record: Draw the animal you liked being best, and how they move.

flow.do: Call out each animal. Your child moves like them for 30 seconds: a sparrow (hops with both feet), a pigeon (walks one foot at a time), a cow (walks on hands and feet), a fish (arms by the sides, wiggling), a snake (slides on the tummy), a crow (flaps, then walks).
flow.say: Be a sparrow! Sparrows hop with both feet together. Now be a pigeon. Pigeons walk one foot at a time.
flow.kid: Be a sparrow. Hop! Now be a pigeon. Walk!
flow.parent: Sparrows mostly hop. Pigeons walk. Crows both walk and hop. Watch the birds at the window and check.

flow.do: Take turns: one person moves like an animal, and the others guess.
flow.say: Which animal am I? How do you know?
flow.kid: Move like an animal. Can they guess?

ask.q: How did you know I was a snake?
good: Because you had no legs and slid along.
Because you moved your whole body.

check.q: Which animal moves with no legs?
check.why: A snake has no legs. The snake moves by bending their whole body and pushing against the ground.

setup.caption: 1. Hop like a sparrow.

setup.art: A boy lying on his tummy, sliding like a snake, while a girl guesses.
setup.caption: 2. Move like an animal. The others guess.

activities.title: Pet, Farm or Wild?
activities.context: In this activity you draw animals you have seen near home and sort them into three groups: pets, farm animals and wild animals. Some are tricky.

materials.item: 12 small pieces of paper
three plates or three circles drawn on paper
pencils or crayons

schedule.what: Draw 12 animals you have seen. Sort them into pet, farm and wild. Talk about the tricky ones.

activities.record: Draw the three circles and the animals in each.

flow.do: Help your child draw 12 animals they have seen, one on each paper. Include a street dog, a pigeon, a crow, a cow, a gecko and a cat.
flow.say: Draw animals you have seen near home. One on each paper.
flow.kid: Draw 12 animals you have seen.

flow.do: Label the plates Pet, Farm and Wild. Your child sorts each drawing and says why.
flow.say: Where does the crow go? Why?
flow.kid: Put each animal on a plate. Say why.

ask.q: The gecko lives in our home. Is the gecko a pet?
good: No, nobody feeds the gecko. The gecko is wild.
Wild, because the gecko finds their own food.

flow.do: Talk about the tricky ones: a street dog, a cow walking on the road, a parrot in a cage.
flow.say: A street dog is fed by the whole lane. Is she a pet, or wild? What do you think?
flow.kid: Is a street dog a pet or wild? Why?
flow.parent: There is no single right answer for a street dog. Some people say community dog. The important thing is the reason your child gives.

check.q: A crow lives on the water tank of your building. What kind of animal is the crow?
check.why: Nobody owns or feeds the crow. The crow finds their own food and home, so the crow is wild, even in a city.

setup.caption: 1. Draw the animals you have seen.

setup.art: Three plates labelled pet, farm and wild, with the drawings sorted onto them.
setup.caption: 2. Sort them onto three plates.

activities.title: Feather and Water (if you find a feather)
activities.context: If you find a feather on the balcony or on a walk, this activity shows how a feather keeps water off a bird.

materials.item: a feather you have found
a small piece of paper towel or newspaper
a spoon of water

activities.safety: Hold the feather by the end and wash your hands after.

schedule.what: Drip water on a feather and on paper. Compare.

activities.record: Draw the feather and the paper, with the water drops.

flow.do: Lay the feather and the paper side by side on a plate. Ask your child to guess.
flow.say: We will drip water on both. What will happen to the drops? Why?
flow.kid: Drip water on both. What will happen? Guess first.

flow.do: Drip three drops of water on the feather and three on the paper. Watch.
flow.say: Look at the drops. Which ones soak in? Which ones roll?
flow.kid: Drip the water. Watch the drops.
flow.parent: On most feathers, the drops stay round and roll off. On the paper they soak in. Feathers hook together tightly, and birds spread oil on them from a spot near the tail. If the drops soak in, the feather may be dirty or fluffy down. Try a bigger, smooth feather, such as a pigeon's wing feather.

flow.do: Talk about it.
flow.say: Why does a crow need feathers that keep water off?
flow.kid: Why does a crow need dry feathers?

check.q: The water rolled off the feather but soaked into the paper. Why is this useful for a bird?
options: It keeps the bird dry and light in the rain
It helps the bird lay eggs
check.why: Wet feathers are heavy and cold. Feathers that shed water keep a bird light enough to fly and warm in the rain.

setup.caption: 1. Lay out the feather and the paper.

setup.art: Round water drops sitting on a feather, and wet patches soaking into paper.
setup.caption: 2. Drip water on both and compare.

activities.title: Fish Tank Watch (if you can visit one)
activities.context: If a friend has a fish tank, or you pass an aquarium shop, this activity is a chance to watch which fin a fish moves, and when.

materials.item: a fish tank to watch, at a friend's home or an aquarium shop
paper and a pencil

schedule.what: Watch one fish for seven minutes. Note which fins move when the fish swims, turns and stops.

activities.record: Draw one fish with all their fins. Draw an arrow on the fin that moves the most.

flow.do: Choose one fish. Count their fins together.
flow.say: Let's count this fish's fins. One on the back, one on the tail, two on the sides...
flow.kid: Pick one fish. Count the fins.

flow.do: Watch the fish swim fast, turn and stop. Notice which fins move.
flow.say: Which fin moves when the fish swims fast? Which fins move when the fish stops?
flow.kid: Watch the fish. Which fin moves most?
flow.parent: Most fish swim forward by sweeping the tail fin from side to side. The side fins flutter to turn, to stay still and to stop.

flow.do: Talk about what you saw.
flow.say: What did the side fins do when the fish stopped?
flow.kid: What did the side fins do?

check.q: Which fin pushes most fish forward?
check.why: Most fish sweep their tail fin from side to side to push forward. The other fins keep the fish upright and help them steer and stop.

setup.caption: 1. Pick one fish and count their fins.

setup.art: A drawing of a fish with an arrow on the tail fin and small arrows on the side fins.
setup.caption: 2. Draw the fish. Mark the fin that moves most.

projects.title: My Animal Comparison Book
projects.context: In this three-day project you make a small book. Each day you draw one animal you saw and fill in their covering, legs, wings or fins, and whether they are a pet, a farm animal or wild.

materials.item: 3 sheets of paper folded in half and stapled, to make a small book
pencils or crayons

schedule.what: Make the book. Draw an animal you saw today. Fill in the covering, legs and wings or fins.
Draw a second animal, very different from the first. Fill in the same things.
Draw yourself on the last page. Compare all three: what is the same, what is different?

projects.record: The finished book, with three pages filled in.

flow.do: 1. Fold and staple the paper into a book. 2. On page one, your child draws an animal they saw today. 3. Under it, write: covering, number of legs, wings or fins, pet or farm or wild.
flow.say: Which animal did you see today? Draw them. Now, what covers their body?
flow.kid: Draw an animal you saw. Fill in each line.

flow.do: On day two, your child draws a second animal, very different from the first.
flow.say: Find an animal that is very different from the first one. How are they different?
flow.kid: Draw a very different animal. What is different?

flow.do: On day three, your child draws themselves on the last page and fills in the same lines.
flow.say: Now draw yourself. What is your covering? How many legs? Do you have wings or fins?
flow.kid: Draw yourself. Fill in your lines too!

ask.q: Which animal in your book is most like you?
good: The dog, because we both have hair and are mammals.
The crow, because we both have two legs.

check.q: Which of these is true about you?
options: You have feathers and two legs
You have hair and two legs
You have scales and four legs
check.why: Humans have hair and skin, and walk on two legs. Humans are mammals.

challenges.title: Two Legs, Standing Tall
challenges.context: This is a making challenge. In the Dough Legs test, the dough animal fell over on two legs. Now you design a two-legged dough animal that stands without help.
challenges.problem: Can you make a dough animal with only two legs that stands without help for a count of ten?
constraints: Use only atta dough or clay and two toothpicks or sticks.
The legs must be the same length.
You may not lean the animal on anything.
materials: two toothpicks, ear buds or broom sticks of the same length
a wooden board, a thick book or a table top
general: Give the legs big, flat feet, so there is more floor under the body.
Make the feet with long toes pointing forward and backward, like a bird's toes.
Make the body small and low, right above the feet.
creative: Add a long, heavy tail that touches the ground, like a third leg. Kangaroos lean on their tail like this.
Put the legs far apart, one at the front and one at the back, with wide feet.
challenges.your_turn: Make your own two-legged dough animal that stands. Then tell someone at home how your design keeps the animal up.

flow.do: Read the challenge. Remind your child what happened with two legs in the Dough Legs test.
flow.say: Our dough animal fell over on two legs. Can you make one that stands?
flow.kid: Make a two-legged dough animal that stands!

flow.do: Your child designs and tests. Let them try, fail and change the design.
flow.say: What could you change? The feet? The body? Try it.
flow.kid: Try one idea. Did it stand? Change it and try again.
flow.parent: Wide flat feet, long toes, or a tail touching the ground all work. Let your child find one. Help only if they are stuck after a few tries.

flow.do: Test the best design for a count of ten. Talk about why it works.
flow.say: Count to ten. Did it stand? Why does your design work?
flow.kid: Count to ten. Why does it stand?

good: The big feet give it more floor to stand on.
The tail is like a third leg.

check.q: Which change helps a two-legged body stand without help?
check.why: Wide feet with long toes give the body more floor to stand on, so the body does not tip as easily. A bird's spread toes do this.

setup.caption: 1. Give the two legs big feet.

setup.art: A dough animal on two legs with a long dough tail touching the board behind, like a kangaroo.
setup.caption: 2. Or add a tail to lean on.

items.p: Sort each animal by their covering.
items.a: see items
items.why: A crow has feathers, a dog has fur, a fish has scales, a snail carries a shell, and a frog has bare damp skin. You have hair and skin, like other mammals.
items.art: Six small drawings: a crow, a dog, a fish, a snail, a frog and a child.

items.p: Draw a line from each animal to how they move.
pairs: Flies with wings and walks on two legs
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Fish swim with fins. Crows fly and walk. Snakes have no legs and bend their whole body. Dogs walk and run on four legs.
items.art: Four animals on the left and four small drawings of ways of moving on the right, mixed up.

items.p: Count the legs in this picture: one hen and one cat.
items.why: A hen has 2 legs and a cat has 4 legs. 2 and 4 make 6.
items.art: A hen and a cat standing side by side in a yard.

items.p: Which animal has six legs?
items.why: An ant is an insect, and every adult insect has six legs. A spider has eight legs. A crow has two.

items.p: A bat is a bird, because a bat has wings.
items.why: False. Bats have wings, but they have fur, not feathers, and bat babies drink milk. Bats are mammals.

items.p: Draw the dough animal that stood up in the Dough Legs test. Show how many legs it had.
items.a: A dough body on three or more legs, spread out.
items.why: A strong drawing shows three or more legs spread out under the body, because those stood by themselves.
items.art: An empty box with a small wooden board drawn at the bottom.

items.p: Say out loud, and a grown-up writes it down: why did the dough animal with two legs fall over?
items.a: Two legs only make a thin line to stand on, so the dough tipped forward or back. The dough cannot move to catch itself.
items.why: A strong answer says that two legs are not enough to hold the body up by themselves, and may say that three legs make a triangle.

items.p: Three of these animals have legs. Which one has no legs?
items.why: A snake has no legs. A lizard and a frog have four legs, and a crow has two.

items.p: Label the fish: tail fin, back fin, side fin, scales.
a: tail fin: at the back end
side fin: just behind the head
items.why: The tail fin pushes the fish forward. The back fin keeps the fish upright. The side fins help the fish steer and stop. Scales cover the body.
items.art: A drawing of a fish from the side with four empty label lines pointing to the tail, the top fin, a side fin and the body.

items.p: Animals with hair or fur, whose mothers feed them milk, are called ________.
items.a: mammals
items.why: Mammals have hair or fur, and mammal babies drink milk. Cows, dogs, bats and humans are mammals.

items.p: Sort these animals into pet, farm animal and wild animal.
items: a cat that sleeps at home and is fed every day
a crow on the water tank
a goldfish in a bowl at home
items.a: see items
items.why: Pets live with a family who look after them. Farm animals are kept for milk, eggs or work. Wild animals find their own food and home, even in a city.
items.art: Six small drawings: a cat on a cushion, a buffalo, a crow on a tank, a hen, a gecko and a goldfish bowl.

items.p: Kavya and her friend Arjun live in Kochi. A brown street dog sleeps outside their building. Many people in the lane feed her.

views.says: She is a pet. The whole lane looks after her.
She is wild. Nobody owns her, and she sleeps on the road.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Why? Then say one thing the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks one side and gives a reason, such as 'she is fed every day, like a pet' or 'no family owns her and she goes where she likes'. Then the child says what the other person has right.
items.why: This is a real question with no single answer. Many people call such dogs community dogs: looked after by many people, but owned by no one family.

items.p: Which one is a mammal?
items.why: A cow has hair, and her calf drinks her milk, so a cow is a mammal. A hen has feathers and a crocodile has scales, and both lay eggs.

items.p: You are an animal.
items.why: True. Humans are animals. We are mammals, with hair, and our babies drink milk.

items.p: Draw an animal you saw today. Colour their covering carefully.
items.a: Any real animal, with their covering drawn: feathers, fur, scales, a shell or bare skin.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the covering clearly, such as feathers on a crow or fur on a dog, and has the right number of legs.

items.p: An Indian pangolin is covered in scales, and the mother feeds her baby milk. Which group is the pangolin in?
items.why: Animals whose babies drink milk are mammals. The pangolin is a mammal with scales instead of fur. One body part alone does not tell you the group.

items.p: Every animal that lives in water is a fish.
items.why: False. Dolphins live in water but are mammals. Crabs, frogs and turtles live in water too, and none of them is a fish.

items.p: Draw a line from each animal to the number of legs they have.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Spiders have 8 legs, insects like the ant have 6, cows have 4, birds have 2, and earthworms have none.
items.art: Five animals on the left and five numbers on the right, mixed up.

items.p: Three of these are insects. Which one is not an insect?
items.why: A spider has eight legs, so a spider is not an insect. Butterflies, ants and houseflies have six legs, like every adult insect.

items.p: A penguin has wings but cannot fly. Why is a penguin still a bird?
items.a: A penguin has feathers, a beak and two legs, and lays eggs. Only birds have feathers.
items.why: A strong answer names feathers, because every bird has feathers and no other animal does. Flying is not what makes a bird.

items.p: A spider and an ant meet on the wall. How many legs do they have together?
items.why: A spider has 8 legs and an ant has 6 legs. 8 and 6 make 14.

items.p: Draw a fish with all their fins. Draw an arrow on the fin that pushes the fish forward.
items.a: A fish with a tail fin, a back fin and side fins, and an arrow on the tail fin.
items.why: Most fish push forward by sweeping the tail fin from side to side. A strong drawing has the arrow on the tail fin.

items.p: Put these animals in order, from fewest legs to most legs.

items.p: Meenakshi's grandmother in Madurai keeps a green parakeet in a cage. The parakeet copies her voice.

views.says: The parakeet is happy. She talks to me and eats well.
Parakeets live in big flocks and fly far. A cage is too small.
In India it is against the law to keep wild Indian birds like parakeets. Some small parrots, such as budgies from Australia, are bred in cages as pets.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Give one reason. Then say one thing another person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks one view and gives a reason, for example that parakeets fly in flocks, or that the law protects wild birds. It also says one thing another person has right, such as the grandmother caring for the bird.
items.why: People really disagree about keeping birds. The Wildlife Protection Act of 1972 protects wild Indian birds, so catching and keeping them is against the law.

items.p: Sort these animals: which lay eggs, and which have babies that drink milk?
items.a: see items
items.why: Birds and lizards lay eggs. Mammals, like cows, goats and humans, feed their babies milk.
items.art: Six small drawings: a hen, a cow, a crow, a goat, a gecko and a mother with a baby.

items.p: Label the crow: beak, feathers, wing, two legs.
a: beak: at the front of the head
items.why: A crow, like every bird, has a beak, feathers, two wings and two legs.
items.art: A drawing of a crow from the side with four empty label lines.

items.p: In the Roll Stopper test, a floating bottle rolled over when flicked. What happened when a fin was taped on underneath?
items.why: The fin pushes against the water when the bottle starts to roll, so it rocks and stops. A fish's back fin does the same job.

items.p: A spider has eight legs, so a spider is not an ________.
items.a: insect
items.why: Every adult insect has six legs. Spiders have eight, so spiders are not insects.

items.p: A whale has fins, but a whale breathes air, like you.
items.why: True. Whales and dolphins breathe air through a blowhole on the top of the head. They are mammals.

items.p: Say one way a crow and you are the same, and one way you are different.
items.a: We both walk on two legs. A crow has feathers and wings, and I have hair and no wings.
items.why: A strong answer gives a real body part that is the same, such as two legs or two eyes, and one that is different, such as feathers or wings.

items.p: A three-legged stool never rocks, even on a bumpy floor. A four-legged chair sometimes rocks. Why do you think this is?
items.a: Three legs always all touch the floor, even if it is bumpy. With four legs, if one leg is short or the floor is bumpy, one leg lifts and the chair rocks.
items.why: A strong answer says that three feet can always all touch the ground. This is why old milking stools often had three legs.

items.p: Revathi and her friend Sana argue about legs.

views.says: Four legs are best. You can stand still without falling, like a cow.
Two legs are best. Your hands are free to carry things, like we do.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Give a reason from the Dough Legs test or from animals you know. Then say what the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks one side with a reason, such as 'four legs stand still easily, as the dough test showed', or 'two legs leave hands free'. It also says what the other side has right.
items.why: Both have a real point. Four legs are steadier. Two legs leave the arms free, but the body must keep balancing.

items.p: An animal has scales and four legs, and lays eggs on land. Which animal could this be?
items.why: A gecko has scales and four legs, and lays eggs on land. A fish has no legs. A frog has bare skin, not scales, and lays eggs in water.

items.p: Three of these are mammals. Which one is not a mammal?
items.why: A penguin is a bird, with feathers, and lays eggs. Bats, dolphins and humans are mammals, and their babies drink milk.

items.p: Invent an animal that lives on a steep rock wall. Draw their feet, and show how they hold on.
items.a: A made-up animal with feet that grip, such as sticky toes, hooks or many legs.
items.why: A strong drawing shows a real way to hold on, such as tiny hairs like a gecko's toes, or hooked claws like a squirrel's.
items.art: An empty box with a steep rock wall drawn on one side.

items.p: Fish scales and snake scales are made of the same material.
items.why: False. Snake scales are made of keratin, like your nails. Fish scales are made of a bony material. They look alike, but are made differently.

items.p: Guess: if the fin on the floating bottle sticks up into the air instead of down into the water, will the fin still stop the rolling? Why?
items.a: No, or much less. The fin works by pushing against the water. Air is much thinner than water, so a fin in the air hardly pushes.
items.why: A strong answer says the fin must be in water to work, because water pushes back much harder than air. A fish is under water, so all of their fins work.

items.p: An ant walking keeps three legs on the ground at a time. An ant has six legs. How many legs are in the air?
items.why: 6 take away 3 is 3. The three legs on the ground make a triangle, so the ant does not tip over while walking.

items.p: Match each body part to the right animal.
pairs: Toes spread, three forward and one back
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Geckos grip walls with tiny hairs on their toes. Crows grip branches with spread toes. Fish push with a tail fin. Cows walk on hard hooves.

items.p: Put these animals in order, from most legs to fewest legs.
items.why: A millipede has many legs, a spider 8, an ant 6, a goat 4, a sparrow 2 and a snake none.

items.p: Write the job of each fin: tail fin, back fin, side fins.
a: tail fin: pushes the fish forward
back fin: stops the fish rolling over
items.why: Each fin does a different job. The Roll Stopper test showed what a back or belly fin does.
items.art: A fish drawn from the side, with three empty label boxes beside the tail fin, the back fin and a side fin.

items.p: Your hair, your nails and a crow's feathers are all made of the same material, called ________.
items.a: keratin
items.why: Hair, nails, feathers, horns and the scales of snakes and lizards are all keratin, shaped in different ways.

items.p: Sort these animals: insect, or not an insect?
items.a: see items
items.why: Ants, butterflies and mosquitoes have six legs. Spiders have eight, centipedes have many, and earthworms have none.

items.p: Lakshmi, a girl in Class 2, says: 'All animals with wings are birds.' Which animal shows that she is wrong?
items.why: A butterfly has wings but is an insect, with six legs and no feathers. Crows and peacocks are birds, so they do not show she is wrong.

items.p: Two cats look the same. One lives in a flat and is fed by a family. The other lives in the lane and catches rats. Is one of them a different kind of animal? Which one is a pet? Give a reason.
items.a: No, they are the same kind of animal. The cat in the flat is a pet, because a family feeds and looks after her. The lane cat finds her own food.
items.why: A strong answer says that being a pet depends on how an animal lives, not on what kind of animal she is.

quiz.p: Which animal is covered in feathers?
quiz.why: A pigeon is a bird, and every bird has feathers. A cat has fur, and a frog has bare skin.

quiz.p: How many legs does a spider have?
quiz.why: A spider has eight legs. Insects, like ants, have six. If you said 6, you were thinking of insects.
A rohu is a fish, and fish swim with fins. Goats walk on four legs, and sparrows fly with wings.

quiz.p: In the Dough Legs test, which dough animal stood without help?
opts: The one with three legs spread out
The one with two thin legs
quiz.why: Three legs spread out stood, and one leg or two thin legs fell over. Three feet make a triangle to stand on.

quiz.p: A crow lives on the roof of a building in Hyderabad. What kind of animal is the crow?
quiz.why: The crow finds their own food and home, and nobody owns them. Wild animals live in cities too.
Humans have hair, and our babies drink milk, so we are mammals, like cows and dogs.

quiz.p: A butterfly has wings. How many legs does a butterfly have?
quiz.why: A butterfly is an insect, so a butterfly has six legs. Wings do not make an animal a bird.

quiz.p: What does the fin on a fish's back do?
opts: Keeps the fish from rolling over
quiz.why: The back fin pushes against the water when the fish starts to roll, like the fin on the floating bottle. The tail fin pushes the fish forward.

quiz.p: When you stood still with your eyes shut, what did your feet and ankles do?
opts: Kept making tiny moves to keep you up
quiz.why: Your feet and ankles keep making tiny moves to catch you before you tip. With your eyes shut, you sway more, so you feel them more.

quiz.p: A green parakeet lives in a forest in Kerala. What kind of animal is the parakeet?
quiz.why: The parakeet lives on their own and finds their own food, so the parakeet is wild. In India the law protects wild birds like parakeets.

quiz.p: What is your own body covered in?
quiz.why: Your body is covered in skin, with hair growing out of it. Like other mammals, you have hair.

maths.problem: Two crows and one dog are standing on the street. How many legs are there in all?
maths.explain: Each crow has 2 legs, so two crows have 2 and 2, which is 4. The dog has 4 legs. 4 and 4 make 8.
maths.context: This is about counting the legs of animals you can see.
maths.why_maths: Adding up legs helps us count animals quickly, even when they are mixed together.

maths.problem: Three ants walk across the kitchen floor. How many legs is that?
maths.explain: Each ant has 6 legs. 6 and 6 is 12, and 6 more is 18. That is three groups of 6.
maths.context: This is about the Count an Ant's Legs activity, where you counted the six legs of one ant.
maths.why_maths: When every animal of one kind has the same number of legs, we can count in equal groups.

maths.problem: A spider has 8 legs and an ant has 6 legs. How many more legs does the spider have?
maths.explain: Count up from 6 to 8: 7, 8. That is 2 more. So the spider has 2 more legs than the ant.
maths.context: This is about comparing a spider and an insect.
maths.why_maths: Comparing numbers shows us one clear way a spider and an insect are different.

maths.problem: In the Dough Legs test, the dough animal fell over on 1 leg and on 2 legs. It stood on 3, 4 and 6 legs. What is the smallest number of legs that let it stand? What do you think would happen with 5 legs?
maths.answer: 3 legs. With 5 legs, it should stand too, but we would need to test it.
maths.explain: 1 and 2 fell. 3 is the smallest number that stood. Every number bigger than 3 also stood, so 5 should stand as well. A test would tell us for sure.
maths.context: This is about the Dough Legs test, where you gave a dough animal more and more legs.
maths.why_maths: Spotting a pattern in our results lets us predict a result we did not test.

science: Cambridge Primary Science Learner's Book 2 (2nd edition), Unit 4.1 'Comparing animals': mammals have hair or fur, birds have feathers, humans are mammals, counting legs of small animals.
Keratin in hair, nails, feathers, horns, claws and reptile scales; fish scales are bony (elasmoid scales of bone and collagen). Any zoology textbook.
Static stability: a body stands when its centre of mass is above its base of support; three spread feet make a stable triangle. Insects walk with an alternating tripod gait.
Human quiet standing involves continuous postural sway and corrections by ankle muscles, using touch, the inner ear and vision; sway increases with eyes closed (the Romberg test).
Fish fins: the caudal fin gives most thrust in most fish; dorsal and anal fins resist rolling; pectoral fins steer and brake.
House geckos (Hemidactylus) make clicking calls, grip with keratin setae on their toe pads, and can drop their tails (autotomy). Birds and reptiles pass uric acid as a white paste.
Eumillipes persephone, a millipede with 1,306 legs: Marek and others, Scientific Reports, 2021.
Indian pangolin (Manis crassicaudata): a mammal with keratin scales; the young ride on the mother's tail.
Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, India: protects native birds, including parakeets and munias, from being caught or kept.

Aristotle, History of Animals: dolphins and whales breathe air and suckle their young. Linnaeus, Systema Naturae, 10th edition (1758): whales placed in Mammalia. Maurice v. Judd, New York, 1818: the jury found a whale to be a fish (D. Graham Burnett, Trying Leviathan, 2007).
Feathered dinosaurs: Sinosauropteryx, described from China in 1996.

roots.context: We have compared animals by their coverings, legs, wings and fins, and tested how many legs a body needs to stand. Now we ask what standing on two legs tells us about ourselves.

deep_truth.truth: Your dough animal stood up without help on three or four legs, but fell over on two. Standing on two legs with your eyes shut, you felt your feet and ankles keep shifting. Each shift catches your body before it tips, so you do not fall. So standing on two legs is work your body keeps doing, every second you stand.
deep_truth.habit: We think standing still means doing nothing. But a body on two legs is acting all the time to stay up, and the body decides each tiny shift without you having to think about it.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Dough Legs test, the dough animal fell over on two legs every time, and stood on three or four. Standing with eyes shut, children feel their toes press and their ankles tighten and loosen to keep them up.

three.who_am_i: You are an animal with hair, skin and two legs. Your body keeps you standing, second by second.
three.what_is_life: A living body keeps acting to stay as it is. Standing up on two legs is one of the things your body does without stopping.
three.what_is_this_world: The world is full of bodies built in different ways: two legs or eight, feathers or fins. Each body suits the life that animal lives.

roots.thread: Animal bodies come in many forms: two legs or eight, feathers or fur, fins or wings. Underneath, many of these different coverings are one material: your hair, a crow's feathers and a gecko's scales are all keratin. And every body keeps itself going in their own way. A stool stands by its shape, but a crow and you stand by sensing and correcting all the time. Your feet and ankles feel the floor, and your muscles answer each shift.

teachings.teaching: A posture should be steady and comfortable. Patanjali says it becomes steady when effort is relaxed and the mind rests on the endless.
teachings.link: In the eyes-shut stand, you were steady only because your feet and ankles kept working. Your effort could relax, because your body kept correcting below what you noticed.

teachings.source: Udana 6.4, the Tittha Sutta (Buddhist Pali Canon)
teachings.teaching: Some men who could not see each felt one part of an elephant. One felt the leg and said an elephant is like a pillar. One felt the trunk and said an elephant is like a snake. Each was partly right, and they quarrelled.
teachings.link: In this unit, one body part alone often fooled us. Wings did not make the bat a bird, and scales did not make the pangolin a reptile. We knew each animal only by putting all the parts together.

science.text: When a person stands still, the body sways a little all the time, and ankle muscles correct the sway. With the eyes shut, the sway gets bigger.
Many of these corrections are run by the spinal cord and brain without our attention. Whether the body feels or knows each correction in its own way is an open question.

other_view.view: These quick corrections are reflexes: fixed, automatic loops of nerves, with no awareness needed. In this view, awareness belongs to the brain, and only some of what the body does reaches it.

how_we_found_out.story: For a very long time, many people thought a whale was a fish. Whales live in the sea, and they swim with fins and a tail. But about 2,300 years ago, the Greek thinker Aristotle looked closely at dolphins and whales. He wrote that they breathe air, give birth to live babies and feed them milk, like a cow. Fish breathe with gills and do not feed their babies milk. Still, for many hundreds of years after him, most books called whales fish. In 1758 the Swedish scientist Carl Linnaeus put whales into his new group, the mammals, with cows, bats and humans. Even then, many people did not agree. In 1818, a court in New York had to decide if whale oil was fish oil. The jury said that a whale is a fish! Today scientists agree that whales are mammals. Here is one more clue you can see in any picture: a whale's tail moves up and down, but a fish's tail moves from side to side. To sort an animal, look at the whole body and how the animal lives, not only at where they live.
how_we_found_out.who: Aristotle, Carl Linnaeus, and a jury in New York
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: A whale is a fish, because whales live in the sea and swim with fins.
